forecasts.rationale: The RBA has raised its cash rate four times in 2026 (to 4.60% on Sept 30) and the Sept minutes said it would go further if required. On Oct 28 the ABS reported 4.3% CPI and a 1.0% quarterly trimmed mean, Governor Bullock said inflation would be above the August forecast, and Deputy Governor Hauser said oil is about a third above the August assumption. Against that, both stressed lags from 100 bp already delivered and a slowing economy, and the Board paused after earlier hikes in June and August; after a 25 bp rise, the next meeting brought another rise in 7 of 11 cases since 2022. A hike is a modest favourite, with a hold the clear alternative.

Historically, 7 of 11 meetings after a hike resulted in another hike, suggesting a 64% base rate. The September CPI rising to 4.3% and strong quarterly trimmed mean of 1.0% exceed August forecasts, and Governor Bullock indicated the Board will assess if past tightening is enough, pointing to a lean toward further tightening. Despite 100 bps already delivered in 2026, the upside inflation surprise likely pushes the probability above the historical average, but mixed activity signals keep it away from certainty.

The base rate for consecutive 25 bps rises in the 2022-2026 tightening cycle is about 64% (7 of 11), which provides a moderate prior for a further hike. However, Governor Bullock's October 28 statement framed the decision as an open question ('whether the tightening to date will be sufficient'), and Deputy Governor Hauser explicitly described a 'choice between further tightening and holding,' both of which are notably less hawkish than the September statement's language. The accelerating CPI (4.0% to 4.3%) and trimmed mean at 3.6% push toward a hike, but 100 bps already delivered in 2026, easing labor market and consumer spending, and the RBA's demonstrated willingness to pause (June and August holds) pull the other way. A sharp adverse oil move or a hawkish SMP could push this higher; a dovish surprise in the SMP or a clear signal to wait for lagged effects would push it lower.

The base rate for a hike following a hike in this cycle is about 7/11 ≈ 64%, but recent evidence strongly tilts toward another hike: CPI accelerated to 4.3% (from 4.0%), trimmed-mean at 3.6%, oil prices well above August assumptions, and both Bullock and Hauser signaled the inflation outlook has deteriorated materially and the Board will consider whether further tightening is needed. The September minutes explicitly said the Board would increase further if required, and the September statement used similar hawkish language. A pause is plausible if the Board wants to assess the lagged effects of 100 bps of tightening already delivered, but the data flow since the last meeting points firmly toward another 25 bp rise.

Base rate: of 11 meetings that followed a 25 bp hike since 2022, 7 brought another rise, and 4 of the 6 meetings this year brought a hike. Hawkish evidence: trimmed-mean inflation rose 1.0% in the quarter, headline CPI is 4.3%, oil is about a third above the August assumption, and the September minutes said further rises are possible. Against that, Hauser called it a genuine choice between tightening and holding because activity is mixed. Bullock framed the question as whether tightening so far is enough, and the Board has already raised the cash rate by 100 bp this year. The November Statement on Monetary Policy forecasts and market pricing are unknown, so I treat it as close to a coin flip.

questions.question: Reserve Bank of Australia increases interest rates by 25 bps at the November 2026 meeting?
questions.resolution_criteria:
This market will resolve according to the change in basis points in the cash rate target resulting from the November 2026 meeting of the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) Monetary Policy Board, relative to the level it was prior to this meeting. 

The resolution source will be official information from the Reserve Bank of Australia, including the statement or release from its November 2026 meeting, scheduled for November 2-3, 2026, as listed on the official RBA calendar (https://www.rba.gov.au/schedules-events/calendar/?topics=monetary-policy-board). This market may resolve as soon as the statement or release of the Reserve Bank of Australia Monetary Policy Board resulting from its November 2026 meeting with relevant data is issued.

If the specified rate is defined by an upper and lower bound, the relevant change will be the change to the upper bound.

If the specified rate is changed to a level not expressed in the displayed options, the change will be rounded according to the following guidelines. Increases or decreases of less than 25 bps will be rounded to 25 bps (e.g. an increase or decrease of 10 bps would be considered to be an increase or decrease of 25 bps). Increases or decreases of greater than 25 bps will be rounded to the nearest 25 bps and will be rounded away from 0 in cases of equidistance (e.g., an increase or decrease of 37.5 bps would be considered to be an increase or decrease of 50 bps). Displayed options of "Increase" or "Decrease" will include policy rate increases or decreases of any size.

If the specified meeting is postponed to a date and time before the start of the next scheduled meeting, this market will resolve based on the outcome of that postponed meeting.

If the specified meeting is cancelled, or postponed such that no decision is announced by the start of the next scheduled meeting, this market will resolve to the "No Change" bracket. Emergency changes to the specified rate not resulting from the specified meeting will not be considered.

Following the 2024 elections, Republicans hold a 220-215 majority in the House. Democrats need to gain a net of three districts to win a majority in the chamber. Republicans can lose no more than two districts to retain a majority.

Democrats continue to believe the party remains favored to regain the House majority, especially because they need to gain only three seats — far fewer than the opposition party usually wins in midterm elections, especially when the president's job approval rating is as weak as Trump's is now. The president's party almost always loses ground in midterm House elections, as has happened in 20 of the past 22 midterm elections stretching back to 1938.

Considerations

Republicans this year are defending an unusually small number of House seats that either voted against President Donald Trump in 2024 or backed him only narrowly, meaning Democrats have fewer easy pickup opportunities against obviously vulnerable targets than is typical for the party out of the White House during a midterm election. House Republicans are defending eight seats that Trump lost in 2024, and 25 more that he carried with a vote total no more than 4 points higher than his national vote share.
